rv.q: And an endlessly revived historical drama from 1953 suddenly feels like the freshest, scariest play in town.
This new Broadway production of Arthur Miller's 1953 drama about the Salem witch trials is the best revival of 'The Crucible' that I've ever seen
This production burns with a passion that feels both period-appropriate and thoroughly contemporary.
Van Hove knows how to channel that heat.
This is a definitive production.

In this gut-wrenching, modern-dress “Crucible” — infused with the visceral suspense and the manipulative underscoring of a horror movie — the director denies us any protective distance from the cumulative modern implications of mass hysteria and hypocrisy.
This is the first production of The Crucible I’ve seen in which the devil, which is to say us collectively, is really given his due.
At which point, this Crucible seems less an anatomy of America than a requiem for it.
Van Hove's electrifying and audacious staging achieves what more revivals should: It makes old work seem new, blows away the dust and exposes caulked cracks.

As their nemesis Abigail Williams, Ronan adds a demonic edge to her usual effortless magnetism and is an entirely plausible conduit for mass hysteria. More impressive still is Tavi Gevinson’s interpretation of the wavering servant Mary Warren.

A lone wolf prowls through Salem, Mass., in Ivo van Hove's eye-popping and wholly unconventional revival of Arthur Miller's "The Crucible," that great dramatic cautionary tale about the perennial dangers of a rampant theocracy fueled by ignorance and mass hysteria...But van Hove is not so much inter...
This production of The Crucible is a reminder that Miller's play works best when it's allowed to be what it actually is.
In the final 15 minutes, Whishaw’s John Proctor and Okonedo’s Elizabeth Proctor make us feel the real horror in The Crucible – the choice forced upon them between staying honest and staying alive.
The show tries to have it both ways: As a supernatural spookfest and as a morality tale about mass hysteria and intolerance.
This is a production that can feel somewhat cluttered, which is a strange thing for a van Hove show.
In cutting “The Crucible” off from any recognizable context, van Hove doesn’t contribute.
The devil may be alive on Broadway; The Crucible isn’t quite.

The international cast of director Ivo van Hove's stunning new production underscores the fallout and suffering caused by narrow-minded, punitive group-think world-wide — and does so without obvious contemporary references to cheapen and diminish the viewer's own emotional response.
This production of 'The Crucible' will make you feel as if you have never seen it before even if you think you know it very well.

"Van Hove does not reinvent so much as he distills...The lead performers are most impressive...Ben Whishaw with Sophie Okonedo as John and Elizabeth Proctor share a raw intensity that burns through our collective consciousness long after the final curtain...
What can be written is that van Hove knows how to put on a good old-fashioned fire-and-brimstone spectacle, and he makes us believe it.
Her seduction seemed to burn holes through the delicate Ben Whishaw.
The play holds up. It has power but I believe it would have more if it were less blunt.
Even if, as in the case with this Crucible (playing through July 17 at the Theatre), the results are mixed.

At a time when smearing a neighbor or movie star or rival presidential candidate can be as easy as hitting "send," it's especially troubling to watch riled-up teenagers and self-centered adults point such destructive fingers with impunity.
His experimental, otherworldly approach is ill-suited to mid-century realistic American drama but can nevertheless be electrifying.
While there's a cold distancing throughout the evening that keeps the production from fully engaging, there are still numerous good points.
If all of the disparate pieces of this "The Crucible" never quite fit together — why, for instance, is Whishaw covered in so much mud in the final prison sequences that you can barely see his eyes?
Van Hove's production sometimes gets at this and sometimes gets lost in a welter of staging ideas.
But as played here, it's high on talk, but stubbornly low on impact.
While there are outstanding performances in Van Hove’s interpretation, I never felt the sense of snowballing paranoia I’d been expecting.
Van Hove's faithful production can't patch the cracks in Miller's conceit.
They all do their best within the limitations van Hove imposes.
All you can think about instead is how this play has finally received its ultimate production, but been destroyed by it.

Instead of immersing us in the uncertainty of the past to the extent that we get a fresh crackling view of our own precarious circumstances, this production, for all the sound and fury spread about the stage and flying in through the windows ends up signifying nothing.
This is a faithful and compelling piece of work, sinister, claustrophobic, and frighteningly real.
The performances are magnificent and give plenty of personality to the characters.
This revival won’t please Arthur Miller purists.
"'The Crucible' is inherently such a powerful play that its strength comes through even when director van Hove gets his hands on it...
This is not lively theatre for the curious tourist or the restless attention span.
But it also tends drown out the subtlety of the human drama, leaving little room for the nuances that make the characters actually feel human.
As Abigail Williams, Saoirse Ronan disappoints; her stage presence falls short of the powerful impression she makes onscreen.
I left the theatre largely disappointed, expecting the brilliance of A View from the Bridge to repeat itself, but this new-concept Crucible lacked clarity and cohesion.
It makes them empty, because you've taken out what makes that play that play, if that even makes sense.
Now his take on Miller’s fifth play – THE CRUCIBLE – is sterile, low-octane slow, badly staged, an assault on eyes and ears as well as horribly misconceived.

cn.t: Van Hove's divisive production of Miller's classic features powerhouse performances from Whishaw, Ronan, and Okonedo, but critics split sharply on the director's unconventional staging choices—some find it mesmerizing, others bewildering.

sg.ra: Intimate 975-seat house with curved rows reducing angle loss. Rows D-H sit ahead of the mezzanine overhang (which starts at row H-J per TickPick/SeatPlan) and are past the stage-height issue reported at row B-C ('stage is high when sitting in the second row center orchestra, so you miss some upstage action' — Headout). JK's TheatreScene confirms Row J still delivers 'full view of the action' for Hadestown including turntables/elevators.

Most expensive rows in the theater. Delivers immersion but SeatPlan reviewer at C8 (6' tall) warns 'usual up-close view where you are looking up at the action,' and Headout echoes 'stage is high when sitting in the second row center orchestra, so you miss some upstage action.' For Hadestown's turntables and upstage balcony effects this is a real trade-off.

Sits fully under the mezzanine overhang (begins H-J) and the orchestra rake is notably shallow — AVFMS/SeatPlan reviewer at N116 explicitly calls out 'rake in the orchestra is not great,' meaning head-blocking from patrons in front is a real issue. Combined with the overhang cutting top-of-stage for Hadestown's upper balcony set, these seats underperform their price.

Rows curve toward stage per SeatPlan, mitigating the side-angle penalty. JK's TheatreScene (Oct 2025) bought J15 for Hadestown at $139, called it 'plenty of leg room' and praised full band visibility plus upstage action (turntable/elevator effects 'perfect from this perspective') because row J sits just ahead of the overhang. TickPick echoes: right side better for band and Hades' balcony visibility than left. Only isValuePick in this dataset.

Multiple sources converge: TickPick says Center Mezz 'promises some of the best views in the Walter Kerr Theatre for the show's visual effects and stage revolve'; SeatPlan confirms 'steep rake ensures patrons in front shouldn't block the view'; SeatPlan reviewer davidnewell (Row C, 5'10") reports 'view is fantastic since row in front is much lower.' Critical for Hadestown specifically because the show's vertical staging (Hades' balcony, revolve) reads best from elevated center.

TickPick explicitly flags Walter Kerr's side mezzanine as unusually strong: 'Unlike many Broadway theaters, the very sides of the Mezzanine are not obstructed.' SeatPlan confirms steep rake keeps sightlines clear, and TickPick recommends Right Mezzanine specifically for Hadestown band/Hades' balcony visibility. Genuine budget pick.

SeatPlan: 'mezzanine has a very steep rake, so most of the seats offer a clear view, but the rear section feels quite far away from the action.' Intimate house (975 cap) + steep rake means even back rows keep a clean unobstructed view per TickPick/SeatPlan, but the distance is real. Better bet for spectacle musicals than dialogue-dense plays.

Near-unanimous negative: TickPick quotes a patron calling it 'not a balcony, but rather the catwalk for the spotlights.' TripAdvisor (Gentleman's Guide): 'view was totally obstructed seeing the spot lights... stage was not totally visible without standing up.' SeatPlan: 'lighting rigs attached to the outside of the Balcony and the ceiling' create obstructions, 'B18 also has thin support pillars,' overhang starts at row D (cuts top of stage), and 'legroom at this height is cramped.' Only 68 seats, two rows — avoid unless deeply discounted and the show is vocals-forward.
